title: Content with right action
hook: the mind is content with itself when it acts rightly (Meditations 7.28)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Marcus's exercise of picking the best things you have, and holding them loosely. Your line was what I have.

You return a wallet you found on the sidewalk. Nobody's watching. No reward, no thank-you note, no story to tell at dinner; the owner never even learns your name. And yet you walk away a little lighter. Something in you settles, like a picture hanging straight. Where does that feeling come from, when nothing outside you changed? Marcus Aurelius had an answer, and it's a very short entry in book seven.

Meditations seven, twenty-eight, begins, in George Long's translation: "Retire into thyself." Go inward, not to hide, but to check what's there. Marcus says the ruling part of the mind, what the Stoics called the hegemonikon, is content with itself when it does what's just, and that brings it calm. That's the whole entry. Notice what's missing: no applause, no result. The mind's contentment doesn't depend on whether the wallet's owner is grateful, or whether anyone knows. It comes from the act itself. If your peace depends on outcomes, you're always waiting: for thanks, for the plan to work, for people to notice. Marcus points to a satisfaction fully in your control. You can't make the world reward you. You can do the right thing, and the mind, he says, is built to be content with that. A fair caution: some hear this as smugness, being pleased with yourself for being good. Not quite. Elsewhere Marcus warns against wanting credit even from yourself, comparing the good person to a vine that bears grapes and asks for nothing. The contentment here is quieter. Less a pat on the back, more the click of a key turning in the right lock.
screen: `RETIRE INTO YOURSELF.` · `THE RULING MIND IS CONTENT.` · `PEACE NOT WAITING ON OUTCOMES.` · `NOT SMUG: A KEY IN A LOCK.` · then, large: `CONTENT WITH RIGHT.`

segments.voice: Remember one right thing you did recently that nobody noticed: a dish that wasn't yours, the truth when a lie was easier, patience on the phone. Let the memory settle, without inflating it or dismissing it. If there's a quiet rightness in it, let yourself enjoy it, the way you'd enjoy warm sun.
Vine. Marcus's image for the good person: a vine that bears grapes and asks for nothing. Today's word.
Your line: content with right. No applause needed; the act is enough. Until next time.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often notice the quiet satisfaction of doing something right that nobody sees, and treat it as enough, rather than waiting for thanks or results.

original.note: Greek: the ruling part, the Stoic word for the mind's command center, which Marcus refers to in 7.28.

what it means: doing what's just brings its own quiet calm, with no need for applause, even your own.
what a scholar hears: hegemonikon is the Stoic term for the soul's ruling faculty, seated in the heart in early Stoic theory, which assents to impressions and chooses actions.

notes: Confirm Long's 'Retire into thyself.' as the opening of 7.28, and the paraphrase of the rest (the ruling principle content with itself when it does what is just, and so secures tranquility).
Confirm that the Greek of 7.28 refers to the hegemonikon (to logikon hegemonikon).
The vine bearing grapes without seeking credit is 5.6; confirm.
Early Stoics (Chrysippus) located the hegemonikon in the heart; confirm phrasing in the trapdoor.
